What to say about this game, seriously, what to say without giving it away.   That is, of course, assuming you haven't watched/read anything about it online. I know it can be hard these days. Lord knows I had first heard of this game because I kept seeing notifications for it from Game Theory Live's "Let's Plays". However, I managed to avoid a lot of it because I had stopped watching said "Let's Play" videos. However, I became intrigued when I came across images from the game on Pintrest.   And well, here I am now, hours after the time I needed to be asleep, having experienced some of the game and I find myself doing something I have never done before.   Writing a review. *GASP*  Anyways, I will take this as the amateur I am and tread carefully to avoid spoilers. This a game that practices an exercise is subverting expectations. While it appears to be a dating sim/anime-styled visual novel with a romance plotline hidden in a sub-plot about mundane school life, you'd be wrong. The game is very meta in its thinking, and by the end of it you may very well find yourself asking "WHAT JUST HAPPENED?!?!". I know I did, and I had a good amount of spoilers placed on my lap by a game review of all things.   However, I can also say that I've gamed as long as I can remember. I've played all sorts of things from the old-school hard days of nostalgic glory to varied games of today and it has been years since I've felt like I do right now. The game's design might not be perfect, the sound might be repetitive (but I feel that's by design, you'll see if you play it all the way through), and some of the game just outright gets sort of repetitive...but it's a wild ride I'd gladly take again.   Yeah, I'm sure I'm rambling, but I doubt many will seriously read my review to this point, so I'll keep on with it if you don't mind. The various subplots between the characters are enough that you can figure out what's coming as the game travels torwards its inevitable concslusions, but when you're actually faced with it, it can still feel like a kick in the gut. In the almost 4 hours I spent, I knew what was gonna happen during the first part of the story and was still taken aback when I actually saw it in front of me. In the same part of the story, I had guessed one of the cast's dark secret and found myself still staring slack-jawed at the screen when it actually showed it to me.   The game is a roller-coaster of expectations, subversion, mundanity, and a clever kind of horror that changes what I thought a horror game could be. It's not a game that scares me, no, it's a game that leaves me with more questions than answers. A game that makes me look at my decisions and think that I'm the bad person for making them. And just when it all seems like I couldn't possibly pull myself up from it all...the game ends in such a way that makes me smile as if all the "wrong decisions" I had made were worth it in the end.   In spite of the horrors of the Literature Club, if will likely find myself coming back to it time and time again throughout the years. Is it fun? Not in the conventional sense. It leaves me with a lot to think of...and a song stuck in my head.

If you don't have an OCD that objects to leaving stuff behind, and you like action roguelikes, even if it looks like crap right now you should get it. You'll play a lot of runs before the refund window runs out, and even though I'm currently broke I'd buy it at full price after knowing what it's like.  [h1]My Pitch[/h1] I didn't see the appeal at all (I didn't mind the art style, the core loop just looked generic), but I got it in some bundle a while back and the moment I fired the first shot it grew on me. Sound, animation, movement, it all feels just right, like this game should be the default other 2d are compared to. One of the most mechanically satisfying games I've ever played, with a very simple gameplay loop that can't get tiresome, but it's just too fast to fully enjoy as a beginner.  [h1]My Problem[/h1] It would be among my favorite roguelikes* if I could adjust the pacing. I often need just a small double jump to pick something up that I couldn't even see on time while falling down. I get that you're not supposed to be going up, but if I was a little better at the game (as I'll get at some point) there's no reason I'd ever miss this stuff. It's just something to frustrate new players. Guns could easily be giving a small knockback to act as a double jump, and this game would be in my top 3 roguelikes of all time. It might still be, I just don't have the patience to train to remove this frustration, so I play about a run a week instead of it being my current go-to-relax game.  [h1]*[/h1] Roguelike Is the proper genre, because games in it aim at the same experience as Rogue - eternal dungeon crawling - and having a different approach to get to that doesn't matter. The adventure is all that mattered in Rogue, turn based and ASCII and all the other stuff wasn't the point of the experience. Roguelike doesn't mean like Rogue, it just happens no good replacement term was found yet as the genre experimented away from Rogue's approach and evolved. But if we don't expect all FPS to be 2D, we shouldn't expect roguelikes to literally be Rogue just because the ill-fitting name was never replaced.

Even for Early Access the game is good.  Peers use the term "Tarkov in space", and I can see why . . . ammo is a thing, but not like you need to load every round, it's more simplified than that. However, when you have no gear, the title has provided several ways to balance the playing field while you get a leg up on some loot. Salvaging & a new "Raiders Mode" game mode that drops you & something like 5 others w/ random gear. The new mode can be launched once every 20 minutes . . . also, there's quite a bit of starting cash & gear to get you going.  The PvP / PvE transition keeps the intensity up & there's a great feeling when you get to know the game-play mechanics & know the levels more.  I'd highly recommend running with at least 1 other person you can trust on your side . . . max squad size is currently capped at 4.

I finished the game, and it did not crash on me (Windows 7/64 bit). In fact, it works fine. (Maybe because I turned the subtitles off?)  This game has a 640x480 resolution. You definitely don't buy this for the art, as line art and the 3D animations are uninspired and look old even for the year 2000. The voice work doesn't sound like much at first, but I found it drew me in as the game continued.  The storytelling and general atmosphere transport me straight into a Russian fairy-tale, and for that the game is worth playing. The game has full voiceovers and is DRM-free. It took me 5 hours to complete.  [h1]Mini-Guide (no spoilers)[/h1] [list] [*]As soon as you see grandma with her book, press Esc to get the options. [*]Turn down the music. [*]Turn subtitles off, they're ugly and the game has full audio. [*]Think of it mostly as an interactive movie. Some cutscenes get very long. [*]Also, you may need to talk to the right people in order to be allowed to do what you already know you need to do. (interactive movie -> dramatic reasons) [*]You can do almost everything with left-click, but right-click is examine/search, and you need that at least once. [*]Remember the two previous points if you are stuck! [*]Save regularly. You can't die, but some people have reported the game crashed for them. (I play on Win7. I had no issues, so I think it's been fixed, but I don't know for certain.) [/list] [url=http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=443266731]Longer guide[/url] in the guide section!

My review for this game is long overdue. I bought this game on launch last year. Decent port despite the neglect from Square Enix concerning patches for this game. It's highly recommended that you play this game with a controller, whether it's an Xbox controller or a PS4 controller.  I recommend that if you have never played a meaningful and psychologically deep game, especially for a JRPG, play this game. Do your best to follow the lore and read the conversation between characters in the game. Do your best to not read spoilers, do your best to answer your own questions by just continuing to play the game... you will get your answers by playing more. It's a deep story with tons of action and provides you a major emotional rollercoaster. Nier:Automata is probably the first game that actually got me to shed a tear at the end of the game because it made me feel well connected with the characters. You can say that this game pulls your heartstrings if you get emotionally involved with the game that it plays out like a good book or movie.  Keep an open mind, it's confusing in the begininng, but the story opens up 10x fold. So make sure you play to get endings A-E. Think hard and through with the very end of the game when you make the big decision. Reflect on the story and drama that you endured before making your decision. People that never played the game will never understand the very last ending.  Great voice acting. Great combat. Great characters. Great movement. Great emotional rollercoaster. A game that greatly hit me in the feels.  My Game of the Year for 2017 without a doubt.

Anyone who can appreciate 2D platforming games should play this; it nails every single aspect of its design. - Every gameplay mechanic is taught actively and without exposition, in a subtle but smart way. You don't have to read anything, you'll learn everything you need to know just by playing. Every single room in the game is engaging without being cheap. - The soundtrack manages to be BOTH atmospheric and memorable, with songs that both fit the theme of the level and feature catchy melodies - every single one. No game has done this so consistently before in my experience. - Every boss and NPC has a unique design. The color palette is bright and vibrant but not sore on the eyes. Each villager feels like a real person. The bosses are fun to fight against; they overwhelm you at first but you pick up on their patterns and beat them in a satisfying way. - It uses the Souls series death system: you lose money if you die unless you can make it back to the spot where you died on your next try. In my opinion more games should implement this as it's a great balance between punishing failure and rewarding consistency. - It doesn't overstay its welcome. It's a short and satisfying game you can complete in a weekend. If you read my entire post then do yourself a favor and buy this game.

Now, before you go ahead and count this as a positive review, allow me to tell you that it is neither positive nor negative.  When i first started playing the game, i thought it was terrible, however, i later determined that Robocraft has a play style of its own and can't really be compared to any other multiplayer game like it. The level designs are great for the team play available and suits all types of robots that you can build. The weapons in the game function perfectly depending on your imagination; you want to fire down on everyone on the opposing team? Then you add guns to the bottom of your robot and add thrusters and hover blades to it. The possibilities are only limited to your own imagination.  However, this is not to say that Robocraft is absolutely flawless, the primary issue which i, and i only guess everyone else faces, is the teamwork. The people that you're paired with are always within your tier, however, this cannot be said for skill level. The other issue in regards to the team play of Robocraft isn't of the developers fault, but rather the players. When you're playing the game it doesn't feel like you're part of a team, it feels like everyone is out for themselves and is more like a free for all except you can only kill certain people. Futhermore, the vast majority of the people dont seem to be able to communicate with you when you need help, they just ignore you.   So, if you're looking for a game where you can drive whatever your mind can think of, Robocraft is for you, just keep in mind that you shouldn't expect too much out of your team, they may as well just be the distraction for you to move in and do your business.

I wish there was an "Ehh..." option under "Do you recommend this game?", because that kinda perfectly summarizes my answer to that question.  Let's get the elephant out of the room:  Skyrim is old. Really old. Expect jank, and lots of it.  That said, this is one of those games I really really want to dislike, but can't bring myself to. It's a lot like FO3 in that regard. This game is severely broken and nonsensical and just dated in a lot of ways, but such a cultural icon that I think everyone should at least try it.  If you want a good Elder Scrolls game, go play Oblivion. If you want Todd Howard's demonic homunculus child, welcome to the homeland of the Nords.  Skyrim, at its core, relies on its combat loop and, to an extent, its status. Way back in the year 2011, when LMFAO was relevant and God had just created the Earth, Todd Howard walked onto a stage and showed the world a video game with real, unscripted, killable dragons, and everyone immediately came on the spot. Since then, Skyrim has become such a staple of video game cultures that it's just too popular to die, on top of being, as of the time of writing, the latest entry in the Elder Scrolls franchise, excluding ESO.  Once you peel back the cool dragons and funny memes and gamer bro culture, however, Skyrim starts to show its age, and more specifically, how poorly it's aged. Seriously, this shit is lying on a stretcher hooked up to dialysis at this point.  Skyrim's primary issue, in my eyes, lies in its balancing. Despite being an open-world game with a supposed plethora of different choices and potential to really craft your character, it's marred by a more classic system of RPG balancing, more akin to old JRPGs, where if you aren't a certain level or don't have certain armor, or don't Google a build, you end up just not being able to fight some enemies, or having to cheese them. For example, I went into Skyrim completely blind on my first save. I played a sneaky archer-type guy with a side hustle in restoration - the idea was to make him kind of an edgy paladin type who was just so nice he stuck to the shadows just to avoid killing. By the time I had joined the Dawnguard, I found I really liked the armor they wore, so I slapped a set on and went about my business. Then, I encountered gargoyles. Everyone else I talked to said gargoyles were no problem, basically free ores on legs. The issue is, I'm a brainlet who plays nothing but shooters, and most of my Skyrim friends were at least somewhat into RPGs, and quickly pointed out that my build was all over the place.  On one hand, that's my fault for going into an RPG and not trying to build my guy around stats, but instead, story. On the other hand, in a game that promises flexibility and the opportunity to really play a role (as one does in a role playing game), I figure I should be able to build my guy around what he would realistically specialize in and not be penalized for it.  That's my personal experience, but even other friends of mine routinely complain about enemies doing things they just shouldn't be able to, such as having a specific, different animation for sidestepping arrows, something the player simply cannot do, and hurling one-shot ice spikes at players, and the result is a game that's technically open world, if you feel like spending forty minutes dodging ice spikes and whittling down a necromancer that's just a higher level than you, wasting your potions in the process.  A final note on the gameplay, I don't like dragons.  I should rephrase - I love dragons most of the time, but then, sometimes they'll fly in while you're trying to do something else, and suddenly, you have to drop everything to spend a few minutes killing a miniboss. It can get pretty annoying, especially in the rare circumstance that an NPC you need to talk to ends up aggroed by a dragon and unable to talk. I realize this isn't a huge thing, and oftentimes, saving and reloading can fix it entirely, but it's still a bit annoying nonetheless.  The game's story is... Alright. As far as Elder Scrolls stories go, it's up there, but not really the best, in my opinion, and a lot of the problem here is the guilds, and how their storylines aren't really design to intertwine with one another in any meaningful way - For example, I can join the Imperial Legion, and then the Dark Brotherhood, and end up [spoiler]killing the actual Emperor of Tamriel[/spoiler], and it's just never brought up. A lot of the quests are this way, where they're cool on the surface, but don't really affect much. I'm not asking for Detroit levels of cause and effect, but it always feels like the quests just go limp halfway through the action, and I automatically despise any quest that sends me into any kind of cave system.  Mount speed and player speed leave something to be desired, animations are dated, sneaking is too easy sometimes, and as mentioned above, difficulty can be wonky at times. Quests can be repetitive or have dumb stories, but I think despite all its flaws, Skyrim is probably worth giving a go once or twice, if you haven't played it already.  Just, for the love of God, wait for it to be on sale. $40 for Skyrim is a robbery.

[h1] If you can spare 10 dollars, get it right now [/h1]  If you have more that that get it for your friends as well.  I am first going to say before I try and actually do a review, look at my hours on this game, let that give you a feel of the amount of time you can put in and not get bored of it, I play it less than I used to, but I still do regularly.  This is a game that is great by yourself, with friends, or with a friendly group of strangers even.  It will run on just about anything that has been made in the past decade, and the methods of play can suit almost anyone.   [hr][/hr]  Okay with that out of the way lets look at its strengths:   [b] 1. Workshop integration: [/b]  This game takes the workshop in pride like no other game I know. If there is something you can think of doing in a video game there is a non zero chance someone has already made it for you either as an addon or a save/duplication, with its over 1.6 [b] MILLION [/b] items on the workshop.    [b] 2. Creativity: [/b]  With all the tools and pre-made materials available you can build just about anything, from convincing sci-fi spacecraft, to a bathtub dragster, to a fortress, to full animations and rendered scenes. All with the tools that come either as standard or that can be downloaded off the workshop; welding, hinging, posing, lighting, freezing, attaching rocket motors, ect.  [b] 3. Community: [/b]  If you feel lonely but can't get your friends to play, then you have options, a lot of them.  As of writing this review there are currently over 6000 servers open and join-able and almost 30000 people actively playing in dozens of gamemodes. Is the community always the best, no not at all, and I certainly wouldn't suggest letting children get on random servers but if you are old enough to be able accept the possibility of encountering bad people you can have a great deal of fun with all sorts of people from all around the world. If interacting with strangers isn't really your thing, dedicated servers are very easy to self host, or get hosted if you have the money for it, which would allow you to control who to allow onto your server and let you have private games with your friends.  [b] 4. Versatility: [/b]  I mentioned this a bit in previous sections but Garry's mod is extraordinarily versatile, any FPS mode you have ever played has almost certainly been recreated here in some form, and some you may have never heard of or that even originated in this game. It doesn't matter whether you want to mess around free building, create intricate scenes, roleplay, PVP, PVE, race a car, or run around as a lamp shade trying not to get killed, all with well over 30000 different maps you can do these things on. There is almost certainly a way to play this game that you will enjoy   [hr][/hr]   Okay now some weaknesses:   [b] 1. Bugs: [/b]  When you have a game that will allow you to mash together 1000+ different addons from different people at the same time, things can get unstable, I mean the game has an achievement for getting a certain amount of errors. Expect incompatibilities in the form of error messages, missing textures (the famous black and purple checkerboard), and game crashes if you start to have to many addons installed at the same time.   [b] 2. Graphics: [/b]  They aren't bad per say but, well most of them originate from games that are nearing 20 years old, so don't expect ground breaking visuals, especially in the stock game. Although this can be improved at least some through addons.   [b] 3. Jank: [/b]  This game originally came out in 2006, and while its gotten many updates over the years, it has at all times at least a bit of that old game weirdness or jank, the physics are what you might expect was groundbreaking for a videogame in 2004, when the source engine, what this is built on, came out. Many things can feel rigid, stilted, or just plain wrong, there is no such thing as aerodynamics and how firmly things attach together is often changed dramatically just by its weight, don't expect soft bodied physics in your cars, and with only a few exceptions don't expect particularly dynamic environments (many maps literally have separate versions just for night time because time, or lighting changes specifically are not things the source engine at least this version, handles particularly well)   [hr][/hr]   All in all, I love this game, I have spent far too many hours playing it and will likely continue to do so, if you can afford it, try it, you might end up wasting 1000+ hours of your life like I did.

Old WW2 RTS game which marked my childhood and interest in tanks and later WW2 military equipment. For me game has nostalgic feel and i have completed it multiple times.  Gameplay Arcade style of combat  - Units have HP and DMG Realistic armuor elements  - Armor has values, front, side rear, top and guns have penetration values.  Infantry is not very strong but it can work in some situations i leave that to you to figure out, you will mainly use tanks if you can.   Units also die very fast even with HP system it takes 1-3 shots to destroy most targets if shots hit, usually its 1 shot.   Ultimate combined arms warfare. Game has diverse vehicle and artillery system. Not very deep but satisfying to use. You don't build a base but call in reinforcements. Trough campaing after each mission you unlock army branches. Those are  Infantry -Mainline infantry -Assault Infantry -Elite infantry  Tanks -Light tanks -Medium tanks -Heavy tanks -Tank destoryers  Artillery and SPGs -AT guns -Light AA -Heavy AA -Long range artillery -Self propelled artillery SPGs -Rocket artillery  Planes -Fighters -Bombers -Ground attack planes  Super weapon.  Each nation has different units inside each army branch and trough campaign they change after each mission. Each mission has limited reinforcements which you can choose, sometimes after completing objectives you get scripted reinforcements to continue your mission.  In each campaing chapter there are multiple smaller missions and 1 grand operation. For each chapter there is total reinforcement amount. To proceed you need to complete operation, big scale battle with usually dozen reinforcements. All reinforcements not spent on smaller mission can be used here to complete operation. This is a nice mechanic which softly pushes you in to playing more carefully and not wasting reinforecemnts, you might need them for grand operation.   AI is pretty scripted but with very hard difficulty sheer amount of enemies is a challenge at least to me.  In each mission not all army branches are available which is good mechanic. You need use what you have to get job done.  Thus there are multiple ways to complete mission. Tank pathfinding is annoying but it's expected due to game being very old.    Do you want to charge with tanks on enemy frontline in epic battle? Do you want to take attrition approach where you bomb enemy lines before cleaning up with tanks? Do you want to take flanking route? Which units are suited for job?  This questions are what you will be asking yourself before you make your move and micro your army.   Multiplayer servers were shut down.   Overall i recommend this game purely for camping experience there is a good amount of content to go trough and i enjoy this type of gameplay.

I was sceptical of getting this game because the huge moves lists and amount of knowledge needed to play the game seemed daunting. They still are. This game has insane depth and requires a lot of knowledge and practice, even learning a character takes a lot of work. However, I am actually surprised how much fun this game is to go into training mode and learn characters. I've never played Tekken before but I've played a lot of Street Fighter, so I'm delighted that Akuma is in the game, especially with Street Fighter IV mechanics. This really helps players transition over. Learning a traditional Tekken character in training mode isn't as bad as I thought it would be: the execution and combo system are a lot of fun, and although there is absolutely zero attempt at a tutorial or explanation of the game's mechanics, I personally find with practice and experimentation it becomes somewhat intuitive. Moreover, I think it's possible to enjoy this game without knowing everything.  In terms of production value, this game is top-notch. Both Tekken 7 and Street Fighter V are Unreal Engine 4, but Tekken 7 looks MUCH nicer, especially the stages, effects and character models. It has a great soundtrack, a story mode that's had significant effort put into it (at least, compared to Street Fighter) and it has character customisation. Sure, it doesn't have combo trials or a tutorial, but honestly the training mode in this game, moves list and sample combos are a refreshing change from overwhelming and crazy long in-game tutorials. I find that it's much more interesting to play around with the game on your own than go through long tutorials which explain the basics but won't help you get better at the game.  I'm far from actually understanding how to play this game competitively, but even as someone who's Super Diamond in Street Fighter V I don't mind being a complete noob, this is a fun game to play even if you're a beginner. Having guest characters is a nice bridge, I understand the controversy but honestly, for a franchise that is so impenetrable, I hope they continue with these varied characters.  Final thing I'll say is that it's refreshing to have a 4-button fighting game. I struggle to play Street Fighter on a standard pad but Tekken is much more natural in this regard: two kick and two punch buttons. I just wish the moves lists were smaller!

As someone who was first introduced to the tactical side of the Battletech franchise with MechCommander 2, I was excited to hear about the development of BATTLETECH. When I heard that it was going to be turn-based, however, my enthusiasm was tempered. I've always maintained that while the tabletop game was turn-based because it is simply not feasible to represent real-time strategy on the tabletop. MechCommander (1 and 2) made the decision to move the game to real time for a VERY good reason, and it bore out in greater tactical depth, more meaningful choices, and the feeling of actually commanding a BATTLE.  Unfortunately, while this may or may not be a faithful or clever adaption of the tabletop game, it is a disappointingly mediocre, under-designed experience by the standards set by a 20-year old entry into the franchise. The devs clearly did not actually consider the implications of most of the mechanics that went into combat, with the end result being needlessly stiff, janky, and poorly-balanced. I've heard plenty of griping about how the late game is a miserable slog of over-beefed doomstacks of enemy units blasting your lance apart, but even my experience in the early game has been extremely disappointing.  In a word, combat fucking sucks. The existing evasion system (mechs build up stacks of "evasion" by moving, and evasion is used up point-by-point dodging incoming fire) MASSIVELY privileges the AI's swarms of shitty light mechs, which nevertheless will effortlessly dance past the outgoing fire from your own lance (even comprised of EXACTLY the sorts of mechs that would qualify as "light mech hunters" in the lore and other games), while inflicting disproportionate damage on your own units. Because again, every incoming attack consumes one stack of evasion, and with all of the AI's light mechs acting on one turn (since initiative is set in blocks based on chassis weight and pilot skill), they can rush in and focus down ONE of your  own mechs by stripping away all of your evasion stacks and hitting it over. And over. And over.  Lacking any sort of "glancing hit" system (i.e., a die roll that's almost-but-not-quite a hit still does some damage), fights in the early game as an agonizing process of systematically wasting turn after turn stripping down a single target's evasion, only to watch it just BARELY survive, and use its own turn to run away and regain all of the evasion stacks you JUST got rid of.  Also lacking any sort of "overwatch" system to allow a mech to forego its attack and instead try to open fire off-turn means that anything that if your lance gets scattered due to terrain and one of your mechs loses line of sight, you can't position it to, say, provide a faceful of hurt to the Jenner that you KNOW is about to round that corner. Instead you just have to passively sit still and let it run past you to get a bunch of free shots on your rear armor.   Landing hits at long range is also an exercise in futility. It feels like anything more mobile than a fixed turret WILL dodge your fire, forcing you to turn every mech into a close-ranged brawler just so that when the computer's aforementioned swarms of shitty light mechs rush up to you, you at least aren't suffering from the massive "minimum distance" penalties for using a long ranged weapon.   Also, while you are guaranteed to face absolute swarms of light mechs from all but the earliest game onwards, you are restricted to your own meagre four-man lance. You know what MechCommander gave us over two decades ago? That's right-- deployments based on drop weight! Being able to customize your forces to meet different threats in different ways. Instead, BATTLETECH contents itself with a lazy my-rules-are-not-your-rules system that completely stacks the difficulty on the side of the fight that has more units in play.  In short, as much as I tried to like this game, the design problems are so fundamental and so obvious I'm shocked that this product has such a positive rating. Maybe people just don't remember that we've solved these problems, whether by transitioning to real-time combat, integrating a hybrid "real time with pause" or "action points" turn-based, or even just by having more options available within the turn-based structure. But I remember, and it makes me deeply saddened that this project could have been MechCommander 3 instead of Fire Emblem: Robots.  EDIT: Having now completed the campaign, I understand a bit more of why people that complete the game have a sunnier opinion of it.  No, the game does not get better-- it's still strategically shallow and the design flaws mentioned above are still slammed into your face every single turn you take, and every single time that your attempt to do something clever is laughed off by the game engine.  Nope, the reason the game gets better is because at endgame, light mechs stop being in the spawn pools for missions.  Having completed the campaign, and started a new Career (No ability to import your save over? No New Game+ capabilities? Nothing?), I was curious if my experience with the early game would be any better now that I had a completed campaign under my belt. Nope, no chance in hell. The early game is absolute garbage, and I do NOT mean that in the sense that a Mech* game should have a rough early game. You are not making hard decisions on a shoestring budget, making tough decisions about future loyalty, or any of that other stuff that seems like an obvious genre staple.   No, instead, what you're dealing with is FUCKING LIGHT MECHS getting spammed on you again. And the more that you play, the MORE obvious it is how absolutely awful the balance and design around light mech combat is. The AI will gladly rush multiple light mechs out of cover and into the crosshairs of your much deadlier mediums PURELY for the sake of ganging up on and focusing down one of your damaged lights. Why? Because the AI has *no* self-preservation instinct. Every single vehicle driver or Mechwarrior that the AI has is a literally fearless death-seeker outside of pre-scripted "I got damaged so now I'm running away to extraction" segments. The sole surviving Jenner with its arms blown off and ammo depleted by an explosion will LITERALLY opt to rush into melee just to deliver a spite melee to increase the repair cost on one of your mechs instead of opting to eject.   If the AI had to deal with a reverse morale system from your own-- starts at full, ticks down as stuff goes wrong-- decisions and strategic depth could be reintroduced. Do you risk going for the early killing blow on the heavier "lance leader" mech, to demoralize the lighter lance-members? Or do you focus on systematically picking the lance apart from the bottom up, to better secure your flanks and deny them indirect fire bonuses, etc?   Also, other points of contention arise as you encounter them more and more. Not just matters or "This cool, obvious feature is missing" but even things like "This extremely obvious design choice was ignored to make an inferior, stupid design choice". A perfect example is how rear shots work. Rear shots (obviously) target the rear armor, which is UNIVERSALLY thinner than front armor. This alone is a huge benefit that makes some risky maneuvering worth it. In addition, however, rear shots also.... Ignore cover bonuses? The much, MUCH more obvious "Rear shots ignore EVASION bonuses" was overlooked, despite the fact that it intuitively makes more sense that shooting someone in the back has a better chance of hitting them since they CAN'T SEE THE SHOT COMING.   The final nail in this negative review is the genuinely AWFUL optimization. There are story missions-- not emergent procedurally-generated missions, but actual fully scripted NON-OPTIONAL, MAIN STORY missions that drop a modern PC to 10 fps. We have games from ten years ago more graphically intensive than this that had better performance.  A solid 5/10. And that's with a +1 because I love the franchise.

I'm a big Souls nut, everybody knows that. I've spent countless hours on the series as a whole, strarting with Demon's and ending with... Bloodbourne. I couldn't play DS3, not only because my system couldn't play it anymore without dying on me, but it also was a step back after DS2, and just not as fun for me as it was before. I needed a fix, and fast. And i found it in Salt & Sanctuary. Let me get it straight: i love Ska Studios, always loved. I adore their recognizable art design - dark, gruesome, and somewhat cartoony. And this game has it too, but it also has every good aspect that Souls had. But it's not a ripoff, oh now. This game has enough of it's own content to NOT be considerent a ripoff. First of all, this game has covenants too, yes, but now they're called Creeds and they're one of the basis of gameplay. You see, every Creed has it's own special things and specializes in different things. Every covenant even has their own replenishable healing items which act differently, and i'm not even talking about abillity to get into your posession through covenant leader such things as Stamina recoverers, throwable items and buff items, which all replenish when visiting the Sanctuary (but only of your own creed, every other creed's sanctuary will have the items that you may got while working for them). Or, what about combat? It's much more awesome than in Souls. Not only you can do secret COMBOS with almost any weapons, it also has two different ways of parrying (traditional and bloodborne method that actually now works with crossbows too) AND you can attack in air. Leveling Up became much more complicated. Much. More. With every level you now get a Pearl that you can use to get nods in you Skill tree. Each nod has something different, like raising your one stat by one point, up to 3 on one node, or leveling up your specialty in, for example, whips, which also raises your agility by some points. Yes, now you don't need stats to wield someithng, but you need to be more leveled in that category, which even includes armor. I don't really like that much, but it's interesting, at least it's different from souls. Everything in the skill tree, even the ammount of healing items you can carry (you can also raise them at Creed's leader, though, but only for a creed). Also, i could say that this game is really a metroidvania, it even has abillities which needed for progression, like wall jump. Which is cool, i like that. But the most important part in this game for me was it's lore, world, plot, all that. I won't say much but i'm really, really interested in this world. I want to know more. About the island, about the world, about salt, about everything. This game is my favourite "Souls" game right now, and probalby will be forever. I'm deeply in love with it, and i can not recommend it enough. Good work, Ska Studios. p.s. WHERE'S THE DISHWASHER? I WAS WAITING FOR IT FOR SEVERAL YEARS NOW SINCE THAT INCIDENT HAPPENED, WHERE IS IT?!

I can dress like Indiana Jones and whip the f*** out of things. 10/10.              In all seriousness, this is hands down the best MMO I've ever played, and ironically it doesn't feel like one. I've poured every hour I have into this game alone, without friends. It feels like a singleplayer game of massive proportions, with elements of multiplayer. The great thing about the game is that you can play in a variety of ways. Want to solo the entire main game? (Which I did) You can. Want to play through with a group of friends? You can.  The game isn't like any other MMO, your quests don't consist of "track this enemy, kill 10 of these and then collect  these etc". You solve actual, real problems in quests called "Investigation Missions". The game comes with a built-in web browesr for a reason! The game WILL make you think long and hard, as well as outside of the box. (One mission has you learn morse code!) It's an absolute blast and I can't imagine how much more fun (and easier) it would be to solve missions and hunt down clues with friends. However, there are also your typical combat-based missions as well. The game also covers a vast array of themes and atmospheres- you can go from fighting a zombie outbreak to trekking through a scorching desert. If you're a lore-aholic then you'll be in heaven, the game rewards players for having a watchful eye and putting two and two together. There are also many cultural allusions in the game, too many to count- Although a memorable one is a mission chain in issue 6 that's obviously inspired by Indiana Jones (No joke, you can get the outfit and whip, which is pretty useful!). Graphics wise this is a really good looking game, better than most if not all other MMOS- however I do play at 1440p with max settings. Some areas may look a bit worse than others, but the game holds up fantastic. I reccomend to use DX11 with this game, because there are some truly clever uses of it.            Some people complain about the combat, and I didn't like it at first either- However, once I learned the fundamentals and played for a bit, I find it VERY enjoyable. There's a plethora of different weapons and abilities you can assign to your characters, perhaps the most I've seen in an MMO. There are dungeons and raids as well of course, but if you don't have friends (cough cough) it can be hard to find groups and complete them. This is a shame, because the few instances where I do find a group, it's such a blast to fight through the dungeons. The community is fairly small! [i]UPDATE May 26, 2015: DoubleFine have removed GFWL from the game, added Steam matchmaking, and this fixes the infamous "stutter bug" (and also wipes all old saves). ([url=http://steamcommunity.com/app/115120/discussions/0/617336568087988501/]source[/url])[/i]  Co-op Iron Brigade is a lot of fun!  [strike]GFWL is not dead. I had a working GFWL install from playing FUEL, and was up and running in 5 minutes. However, if you haven't, you probably need the updated client, which is here: http://www.xbox.com/Live/PC/DownloadClient You can probably download and install this before you download iron Brigade, or you can install Iron Brigeade, uninstall GFWL, and then install the newer version. Make an account, copy and Ctrl-V paste the serial, done. (GFWL often takes a minute ro more to connect, and sometimes needs more than one attempt.)[/strike]  You need to play two missions in singleplayer; after that, you know the basics of the game and get access to the "radio room" where you can invite friends, search for games etc. [strike]"Friends" means GFWL friends and not Steam friends, of course, so you need to add each other on GFWL. [/strike]You can do in-game text-chat with "T"; [strike]if you have configured speech in the GFWL settings,[/strike] you'll also automatically have voice chat with everyone in your game [strike](if your microphone isn't claimed by Steam)[/strike]. The co-op missions are the same as the singleplayer missions, so you advance in singleplayer as you play co-op.  I like the co-op rules. You need to collect "scrap" (= drops from the enemies) to be able to build turrets; any scrap you collect (or that scrap collector turret collects) gets shared equally (as are the random chest drops), but any turrets you place go off your own budget. You can only build those turret types that you have equipped (they're called "emplacements" in the loadout screens), but you can upgrade any turrets on the battlefield regardless of type. Of course you can revive each other.  Tactics for us was to go into each new map with the same loadout as the previous one, slightly modified by the hints the game gives you. We were only defeated once, but then we do go back and refine our strategy for gold star performance. This means talking about weapon and turret loadaouts, turret placement strategy, fire sectors (very loose), and the like. We were already on the chassis that has a maximum of weapon slots and a minimum of turret slots, but careful planning was still necessary to get that coveted gold star: even at that extreme of the game balance spectrum, you can't just adopt "shoot everything that moves" as a viable tactic.  Game balance is excellent: chassis types allow you to trade weaponry (fps) against turrets (tower defense) -- this affects both the turret types you can equip and their cost. Special skills are equipped via legs, and they're balanced as well: "quick reload" means you're stationary while that skill is engaged; "sprint" means you're fast, but can't turn while running, etc. You need to use your skill wisely, i.e. tactically.  [strike]The "stutter bug": 6 hours into the game, after 7 missions, the game started stuttering when scrap is being collected. That bug is not present in the Xbox version, and the FAQ says that since it seems related to GFWL, it is difficult/impossible to debug, and Microsoft is not being helpful. So that bug is there to stay. Since you can't shoot while collecting scrap, you tend to only do that when no enemies are around, which means the bug is an annoyance, not a showstopper at this point.[/strike]  I got Iron Brigade for free when I bought "Hack'n'Slash", possibly because I previously owned a lot of Double Fine games, including at least one bundle (Amnesia Fortnight). Getting it on sale seems definitely worthwhile even now, [strike]but if you have an Xbox, you're probably better off getting it there, because of the stutter bug.[/strike]  As a game, Iron brigade is exceptionally well designed: it is easy to get into, has tactical depth, and allows for a wide variety of approaches to beating a level that are well balanced among each other, both in singleplayer and co-op.

What is Company of Heroes 2? A freaking mobile game?!  There are SO many high priced DLCs that feel as though they SHOULD have been in the base game. Only two base factions? One short campaign? A decently good multiplayer? Really?   The US Forces are DLC, a second Germany faction is DLC, the British are DLC, the US Forces campaign is a DLC... And they're not CHEAP DLC either. They're selling you DLC for full-game prices. So let me break this down for those who aren't catching on.   Multiplayer DLC                                             US Forces               $13                                                     2nd German Army    $13 British                     $13                                      Campaign DLC US Forces               $40 British next???  Expansions US Forces Campaign, Single squad (FOX) Several missions for the original game  Miscellanious DLC TONS of skins for vehicles TONS of perks that barely boost your performance (highest I've seen is a 3% increase) Several different leaders (different special units and abilities)   You have to buy the US Forces TWICE! Once for their campaign, once to use them in multiplayer! Why?!?! The campaign is $40 as it is, and then you throw a $13 multiplayer charge on top of that? PLUS there's an expansion for the campaign that costs money as well? And it's only a new US Forces squad?   I really do not mind the use of DLC to expand the experience, but it really feels like I'm being ripped off by purchasing CoH2. Even though I got it on a great sale. So now I either buy a $40 DLC, or I live with the fact I bought DLC I literally cannot use.   In all honesty, I enjoyed CoH1 more anyway. There are a few improvements to CoH2, but not enough for me to justify telling anyone to buy CoH2 and ALL the DLCs being made.   Stick with CoH1. Initially, I criticized the developers for resetting the character level for all players. However, after some thought, everything made sense for me. Firstly, the equipment progression system is very interesting. Thanks to this system, you can feel the progress. But if the developers hadn't reset the level for all players, they wouldn't have been able to add this system. It would have been impossible to tie the equipment to specific player levels at a time when many players already had levels ranging from tens to hundreds. And if they had added new equipment without this system, low-tier equipment would have gone unused, and consequently, the new content would have been ignored by lot of players. In future updates, I would like to see new maps. In my opinion, the rounds go by quickly (for me at least), making the maps feel quite repetitive. Either add more diverse maps or more advanced and complexed interactions between the ghosts and the environment/map and players.

JBMod sorely lacks the features and culture of Garry's Mod.  The important [i]Switch physgun modes[/i] is not bound by default, so you'd have to go into the keyboard options and set it to something like T. This enables you to switch to the ballsocket and rope versions of the physgun, but the mechanics of getting it to work is unintuitive and awkward (align the right-clicked bugbaits, hold right-click, let go of left-click, then let go of right-click). There only seems to be one map (jb_buildingblocks), with the exception of a server running some levels from Half-Life 2.  Gameplay is a mixture of clunky (random) deathmatching, and every type of spam imaginable (including props, vehicles, mics, audio files, animations, NPCs). Certain console commands seem critical (stopsound, retry), and particular console commands seem to be the only way to spawn vehicles and NPCs. There's little constructive effort seen, probably due to the lack of tools (and because the tools are poorly designed). It's mostly just madness, but that can be fun in itself.  It was interesting to see the essential foundations of what Garry improved on since 2004, and get a taste of what that early Gmod Sandbox culture would have been like. I doubt the servers will remain populated though, as updates would probably be needed to retain interest, but Gmod is cheap and already far more advanced. The main criticism is that it's too unstable, as it crashes every few minutes. They both originated in Dec 2004, but it would be untrue to say that JBMod is anywhere near as relevant to gaming as Gmod. It [i]might[/i] be worth a glance though.

A Revolutionary Multiplayer Experience! Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)  Grand Theft Auto Online is an absolute masterpiece when it comes to multiplayer gaming. Rockstar Games has outdone themselves by creating a virtual world that is both immersive and incredibly fun to explore. As an avid fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I can confidently say that GTA Online offers an unparalleled experience that keeps players hooked for hours on end.  One of the standout features of GTA Online is its vast open world, which is a detailed and living representation of Los Santos. The attention to detail is truly remarkable, with a stunning range of landscapes, iconic landmarks, and an assortment of activities to engage in. Whether you're racing through the bustling streets, taking on daring heists, or simply exploring the city with friends, there's never a dull moment in this virtual paradise.  The gameplay mechanics are incredibly polished, making it a joy to navigate the world of GTA Online. The controls are responsive, the driving feels realistic, and the shooting mechanics are satisfyingly smooth. The game provides a plethora of options for players to customize their characters, acquire luxury vehicles, and amass a fortune through various legal and not-so-legal activities.  The multiplayer aspect of GTA Online is where the game truly shines. You can team up with friends or join forces with other players from around the world to embark on heists and missions that require coordination and strategy. The sense of camaraderie that develops during these ventures is exhilarating, and the feeling of accomplishment upon successfully completing a mission is unmatched.  Rockstar Games consistently updates GTA Online with new content, ensuring that the game remains fresh and exciting. From new vehicles and weapons to major expansions, the developers never fail to keep the player base engaged and entertained. The active community and the numerous player-created game modes and missions further contribute to the game's longevity.  However, it's worth noting that like any online multiplayer game, GTA Online does have its fair share of occasional server issues and connectivity problems. While these instances can be frustrating, Rockstar Games has demonstrated a commitment to resolving these issues promptly and ensuring a smooth gaming experience for its players.

I mean true rpg, games of choice. Fallout 3 is not bad shooter with rpg elements. Fallout 4 is a shooter with a bit of RPG elements. If you dont care if Fallout is shooter or it is RPG, then you will disagree with me, of course. But me personally, I see Fallout series as RPG games. And lack of role-play, I mean true role-play, in F3-4, it is that makes this games not so good like F1-2 and NV. Also, there are some another things. Majority of players doesnt see them but... I will say about it. You see, Fallout 3, for example, looks like some strange one of its kind. Its not exactly Fallout game like 1-2 and not exactly the Elder Scrolls (hello, Bethesda!. Its pretty strange game speaking of post-war atmosphere and locations itself. Its like you want to make great coctail. But you have no idea how it must be done, only suggestion. So you are taking all components but making them not in right proportion and so on... Fallout 3 has Enclave, super-mutants, radiation and wasteland, but it has very bad portraing of post-nuclear world. Same to Fallout 4. Its a long topic but I will say it in short way: 1) There are lot of buildings which are in not too bad condition and still no one are living in them. Its like its pos-nuclear setting so people have to live in some terrible self-made houses and there must be ruins where no one is living, with no reason at all. 2)There are no green grass/trees etc.  It looks like its 20-30 years passed after the war. But not 2 centuries. But according to the lore, its 2 centuries. There was wasteland in F1-2 because action was taking place in the California. Im not from USA but Im more or less familair with California climate. And DC and Boston... Yes, bombs fell. But 2 centuries! Bombs have not fell everywhere. It means there must be large areas untouched by war. With nature and flora and fauna. And you know, Radiation itself IS NOT too terrific for plants and trees. Look at Chernobyl! Why there are so many dead trees in Boston? If trees are dead since Great War, they must be not just rotten already, they must even not exist anymore, lol.  This environment stuff is so weird just like Enclave stuff in Fallout 3. Enclave was destroyed in F2 but just because its Fallout game there must be Enclave. So lets put them in the game. Like I said - all components of F1-2 just mixed up somehow.  And now lets go back to the Mojave Wasteland. Fallout New Vegas is my favorite game in whole series. Its nice and much complex game than F3. First of all, its not shooter with rpg elements. Its RPG with shooter elements! Here you can make a big variety of roleplay with really different and multiple endings. Its even more adult game. You can gamble, take who.res, take drugs, and in the main quest tou can join Caesar'a legion and make Nevada really terrible place of slavery and terror. Or you can be a knight in shiny armor. A lot of side-quests have good variety of choice as well. Also there a new reputation system along regions/towns of Mojave Desert. You can be remembered as a hero in one town and as some maniac in another. It also works for factions. You are friend of New California Republic and enemy of Caeser's Legion. And so on. And all in-game world is made in logical way. Finally, we can see how society is ressurecting because 2 centuries are passed after Great War. We can meet soldiers of New California Republic. We can visit New Vegas, even it was untouched by war. But anyway, it looks much better than DC wasteland and Boston...   Fallout 4... Well. I haven't played it. I only saw youtube walkthroughts and spoke with friends who played. Well... Its NOT, defenitely NOT good roleplaying game. Its even less RPG than Fallout 3. My friend completed Fallout 3, NV, 4. As he says, NV is good RPG game, and F4 is really bad. There is no variety at all, even endings are almost the same. There are no such variety in role-play and dialogues and so on. I even dont need to play it to see how this game made! I saw new dialogue system. It was enough. There are some good moments in this game, but we cant speak about it like about good RPG. As shooter with RPG elements its OK. There are some things which are really made good, I mean some cut-scenes and so on. For example, all pre-war introduction looks good. Also, I can say same about vault-introduction in F3.   DLCs for Fallout 3 are kinda good. Kinda, because Mothership Zeta and Operation Alaska or whatever its called are just shooters. I find them boring because its not Call of Duty or something like this. Playing shooter on fallout 3 engine and with its mechanics... Not the best choice.  DLC for New Vegas are great. They are giving a lot of original quests (specially Old World Blues), good plot, RPG elements and so on. They are actually connected with major storyline and together with it they are creating complete story about courier and his way throught the conflict in the Mojave wasteland.  If someone read it all, well, I'm pleased. And I will be glad to read what you are thinking about all that.

Great game. Combat is fluid and enjoyable, even more so as you unlock new skills and weapons.  Art style and soundtrack are both good. From infested slums to an ancient vaults, the scenery can be truly fascinating and it's music fits each moment really well.  The game can also be rather challenging in hard mode. I struggled with some bosses and certain areas of the game and had to change my strategy multiple times to defeat them. Both main characters, Vanessa and Monty, are quite charismatic and their hilarious interactions really add up to the experience. There's a fair number of weapons to unlock, each one with its own skill tree, which allows one to choose different fighting styles to face their enemies with lots of stylish combos. While i have never been a sucker for collectibles myself, there's a variety of codices to search for throughout the whole game which expand the game lore. This, together with it's multiple achievements, gives the game some replay value. There's a Coop mode, in which the other player takes control of Monty, the hellhound. I played this on my own so i have no idea how well it works but coop is always a nice thing to have. From a technical standpoint, the game runs smoothly. I didn't find a single bug nor did it crash a single time. Lastly, while i do believe that this game would benefit from an extra difficulty unlocked after beating the game on hard (like a new game + or very hard) to challenge your maxed out character, the amount of content that the it already provides is more than enough to make it worth what you'r paying for.  In conclusion, Obey me is a fantastic Indie game, with fast paced action, a great setting and interesting characters. (Also, Jojo references are always a nice touch.)

ORIGINALLY POSTED: April 2016 UPDATE BELOW  I've never played Darksiders 1 or 2 before, so this is written from the perspective of someone brand new to both the game and the franchise. It's a very fun ARPG, overall. Movement and combat are both fluid, the story is decent at worst, and maybe even good at best. Some specific points, in no particular order, follow:  1. Platforming is easy. You cannot 'miss' jumps, because Death (whom you play) grabs onto handholds and bars automatically, as long as you jump in that general direction. The platforming elements are more of a simple 'puzzle' than an exercise in virtual agility. As somone who sucks at platformers, I loved this aspect.  2. Puzzles are easy. Most of the time the solutions are obvious as long as you explore the surroundings. They're pretty inventive in certain ways, and each puzzle builds on elements used in the last one. As someone who sucks at puzzle games, I enjoyed them.  3. My combos get interrupted when I'm hit. I can see enemies pulling back to strike, but I haven't discovered a method for blocking or interrupting them, no way to continue my combo without either getting hit or rolling away, and starting over. Perhaps there is a way I've not discovered yet, but this is a slight annoyance to me. Only a minor one though.  4. Combat is very fluid and fun - comparisons to God of War come to mind (albeit without the long range of Kratos' chainblades, alas).  5. The game runs smoothly, and loads quickly, with hardly any loading screens at all once you've loaded your savegame from the main menu.  6. It's gorgeous! Sure, it's not gonna win any awards, but I find the game very good looking.  UPDATE MARCH 2017  Now that I've gotten around to beating the game and beginning a new game plus, I can only recommend this game even more strongly than I did before. I've fallen in love with it.  A. The architecture is absolutely epic. The Forge Lands (which comprise the first third of the game, sans the prologue) has plenty of epic structures, but once you leave that area, it gets even better! Granted, this is not related to gameplay, or even the story really, but for me it really added to the sense of wonder and grandeur as I played.  B. The music. OMG, the music. It's incredible. My wife, who isn't really into video games, went out and bought the OST, it sounds that good.  C. I mentioned the well-structured puzzles in my original review, and later on, some even more inventive puzzle elements are introduced. It was really actually a lot of fun.  D. The action is so good. I said it before, but it's worth reiterating. Very responsive, very fluid, very fun and dynamic. You feel like a bad-ass wrecking face.

Sometimes, I can press one of the attack keys and target an enemy and it works just fine - dead enemy.  Other times, my pirate runs dumb, fat, and happy right into their detection range and I have to rewind yet again.  And then, if you press pause to assign orders, you have to press <enter> or click the "Execute" button as quick as you can.  Not good if you hit the pause button to mitigate detection or attacking enemies.  And then, there are times when I give orders in the pause screen and cancel it, but I try to give them orders un-paused and it still tries to execute the paused action (usually running).  Pretty much all of this results in detection, usually resulting in rewinding.  While I cannot recommend or reject this game (Steam requires a recommendation thumbs up or down; therefore, I have to rate it down because it's not the easiest "yes" I'd give to a game), the best suggestion I can give is to play the demo as far as you can.  If you like it, retry the main game here and skip as fast as you can to try to get beyond the demo and play as much as you can within the 2 hour limit Steam allows for returns.  If you're not outright loving it by then, refund.

With all the work that has gone into this title since launch I can finally say that I can recommend this game. The core of the game is roughly the same, but they've added a lot of content to help make the universe feel more alive and to give you more stuff to do whilst you explore. The number of quality of life improvements to the game as well as optimisations make playing the game a much better experience though the massive 1.3 update has introduced some bugs unfortunately. It's clear the devs love this title and want to make it the best space exploration game they can, after all, all these updates have been free (and I pressume will stay that way till the money runs out). Added content since release includes, in no particular order, base building, planetary exploration vehicles, more variety of pretty much everything and probably more I've missed; this also doesn't include all the quality of life improvements. The flight overhaul in 1.3 makes flying your spaceship much more fun, and reworked space combat feels good.  I've left my original review attached so that you can see where this game has come from.  ORIGINAL REVIEW: First off, I like the game, there's not much to do but I like flying around and looking at planets even if it does run like complete garbage. THAT SAID, I CANNOT recommend this game because it was falsely advertised. The game you see in the trailers is not what you get. There are better posts covering why but in short they made up a bunch of features that never made the final product either because they were cut or didn't exist in the first place and we were just sold a load of hot air. These cut features turn this game from deep space exploration game to space sightseeing, which I'm fine with but don't buy if you want any form of depth.

With 53.2 hours under my belt, I have enough hours in the field to give a review which reflects this game's quality.  As a huge fan of the Close Combat series, I was greatly anticipating the release of this game back in May. I was not to be disappointed. The game is outstanding. I am a great advocate for historical realsim in RTS's and Steel Division's reliance on actual aerial photography to depict it's wide range of maps is a great relief.   The AI is almost too difficult at times but no one plays an RTS hoping for an easy time right? I wooped with joy the first time I beat the AI on hard difficulty (yes, there is a very hard setting too). You really have to earn your stars in this game.  The 18 divisions based off iconic divisions of the Normandy campaign are beautifully modelled and are well balanced, A player can have at their disposal air, land and sea (in the form of offshore artillery) at their disposal. The battles are hugely entertaining given their large scope and watching your units battle highly intelligent AI is a joy to watch and command!  Mod support will ensure this game has a long life. The audio mods are particulary impressive and really enhance the atmosphere on top of what is already a very good audio system.  Of course, you can also do battle in multiplayer with as many as 10vs10 battling it out very large maps (map size depends on how many players are involved).  There is a Campaign (12 missions divided between Germany, Britian and America) which is beautifully done with a great emphasis on voice acting and stock footage cut scenes to give the game a historic edge. Skirmish mode is also highly entertaining and where I have so far practised alone to compete with those in multiplayer,  I highly recommend this game and score it 9.5 out of 10.

Difficulty is non-existent, to the point I’m doing dungeons on Hard difficulty and they’re not as difficult as any normal enemies in any other Hack and Slash I’ve ever played. "Now, why is that? Mr. 578 Hours?" I definitely hear you asking, well, aside from the fantastic story mode that the Grand Theft Auto series is well known for, the online component has shown Rockstar that they don't really need to try with making new or interesting singleplayer content - something that the GTA series was known for, and it's a shame that the closest we'll be getting to it is buggy missions added to Online, or yet another Online expansion that has recycled concepts from scrapped Story Mode DLC. Not to mention the massive money farm that Online has become, thanks to not just game sales but also Shark Cards, which allow people to buy money that can barely get them any of the more powerful vehicles. To get one of the most infamous vehicles in online, the Oppressor MK2, one requires purchasing the Oppressor, a Terrorbyte to store it in, and a Nightclub to store the Terrorbyte in, totaling out to about $5 Million in-game, and that isnt even getting into how hard that is to comprehend to new players, or how that costs over $50 in real world dollars, or how other routes for owning and upgrading vehicles are just as expensive and require extensive grinding to even reach (Hence my almost 600 hours, and more that I will rack up after this review).  And yet despite the fact that this game is so lucrative to Rockstar, it feels as if they don't care or are being told not to fix even the most basic of issues by their Publisher, Take-Two. GTA Online is filled with so many inconveniences, glitches, and modders that it can sometimes make the game a joyless slog to play.   [b]In the case of inconveniences, you have:[/b] The slow and clunky snack and body armor system, acting as one of the few ways of healing damage (Thankfully Rockstar is addressing this in an upcoming update, better late than never)   Lack of fast travel even though you can use jobs as warp points, and joining a new lobby will warp you to your spawn  Custom loadout system that allows you to hide weapons you dont use, yet you need to buy a Gun Locker that costs roughly $300K PER PROPERTY  If you experience "An Error" in a GTA Online session, it will boot you back to story mode, and you'll be forced to reload back into online, which takes minutes  The knowledge that if it's a bug that makes the game much harder to play, but doesnt allow you to make money faster, Rockstar likely wont patch it.  [b]You also have lovely bugs that have existed for a shocking amount of time, such as the following:[/b]  Heist Finales not paying what they should (Crew Cuts seemingly reset) Getting stuck on infinite loads Being given weapons or equipment you shouldn't have and can't get rid of Transaction Pending getting stuck for an eternity Your personal vehicle winding up destroyed Social Club refusing to launch GTA 5 because you have an incorrect setting in-game or something in your file structure  [b]Not to mention the abundance of hackers, and Rockstar's negligence of the game's security[/b]. There are so many hackers on this version of the game that it's honestly insane that they havent infested every corner of this game and ruined it for all involved. What's worse though is how Rockstar either can't or simply refuses to implement any form of anti-cheat or improve the security of their net code, all bans are manual which means that unless your account is really suspicious, you can get by scott-free, but also hackers have the ability to see the IP addresses of all players connected in a session, which is a huge security issue (and it doesnt help that Social Club is just as bad, your Rockstar ID literally being associated with your IP and not being an account #).  I hate GTA 5, I hate what it has taught Rockstar, and that Online has shown Rockstar that they don't need to try and make a new and original product. It's been almost a decade since the release of this game, and not much has changed with story mode, and online's missions mechanically have not evolved beyond, "Go from point A to point B to collect C." Online strains aging and dated mission design and art in a game world that could have used an expansion at least a couple years ago. With focus on GTA 5 being primarily on Online, so many new updates have caused a whole array of bugs in Story Mode, breaking the way cutscenes work and causing game-breaking bugs that ruin the airtight polish of Story Mode at release. This is a game that has been ruined over time thanks to corporate greed and a lack of interest in Singleplayer content, which is disappointing in a series about singleplayer experiences. I've been playing this game since launch, I've been around since Xbox 360 and I've seen this game change over the last 9 years, not in terms of mechanics or new and meaningful editions, but watching as yet another great installment in a franchise known for its well-written stories and third-person action mutated into a product of corporate greed and derelict ideas being wasted, and Rockstar - or more accurately at this point, Take-Two - has shown no signs of changing this formula.  Would I recommend this game to someone else? If you're in it for Story Mode, then absolutely, but the Online component I would only recommend if you have other friends willing to play it with you, otherwise, stay away, and don't give Rockstar/Take-Two your money until they prove that they can make something worth your time.  Outdated Review (January 24th, 2023) - Made during the Security Leaks of early 2023 In lieu of the recent bugs and exploits made available by the GTA 5 source code leak, I would not recommend this game under any circumstance; It's simply too risky to play in the current ecosystem. Either Rockstar needs to consider some form of Anti-Cheat, or find some way to close off these exploits from an end user. [i]Her Story[/i] is an FMV title that plays as a mystery story.  [i]Her Story[/i] is unique among the FMV class of games in that its story is not a linear progression; it is a series of clips presented in whichever order the player finds them.  To find clips, the play enters a keyword or collection of keywords, much like searching in an Internet search bar.  All clips are of a woman being interviewed by the police over several days.  Most FMV games play as a linear story with some elements of choice.  [i]Her Story[/i]'s method of storytelling is unique and creates a narrative experience unlike any other.  The story is not placed in front of the player; the player searches for the story.  Driven by their own curiosity, the player pieces the story together until they are satisfied.  This experience simply would not be possible in a simple movie or a traditional game.  It can only really be told in the medium [i]Her Story[/i] uses.  This game demands the player's interest and rewards their curiosity with an intriguing tale.  [i]Her Story[/i] is not for everyone.  There is no action.  There is no gore, no bullets, no zombies.  There are no flashy graphics or powerful soundtrack.  It is only the player and the woman.  It is all about her story.  The story is fun and interesting, but it is not an epic tale.  [i]Her Story[/i] will not make the player say "Wow!"  It will make the player give a fascinated declaration of "Huh!"  For those willing to let their own interest drive their experience in the story, [i]Her Story[/i] will surely be a novel experience.

If you loved Outer Wilds or Return of the Obra Dinn, you'll love this too - it's in the same vein of puzzle-solvers that you can only play once.   Note: the game has two flaws, one I found to be majorly unfun and one I only found a bit annoying. The major flaw: the forced stealth segments. These suck, though they aren't so frequent that they ruin the game. LATEGAME SPOILERS: [spoiler] It was especially aggravating that the "final boss" was basically a series of stealth segments. [/spoiler] The much more minor flaw was that sometimes, elements in the game world that were needed to solve puzzles would be very difficult to notice, and that led to a lot of backtracking and wandering trying to find something.  Overall: if Outer Wilds and Obra Dinn are 10/10, then this is a 9.75, losing a quarter point for forced stealth. It's honestly offensive that this is only 20 bucks. Play it, you must.

It was a long four months driving back and forth to work and the hospital. During this time, I suggested we play something to take our mind off of our circumstances if only for an hour or so. She reluctantly agreed and I picked out sackboy. At the time, I had a PS5 which I sold later to cover some medical bills. We loved the entire experience. The music levels are brilliant and I couldn't help but smile everytime we jumped into craft world. It can be a tougher game, but its really worth it. My wife played and she had no real gaming experience so i don't mind recommending it to gamers of any level! The graphics are gorgeous, the music is sublime, and it's endlessly fun. I'm playing it now on my steamdeck while my son is asleep at night. I bought it on sale, but I would have paid full price both times for it considering my nostalgia with it. I hope you enjoy from my family to yours.  Joe

No Mans's Sky is a game I overlooked until a couple years after it was released. All of the hype surrounding it before launch and the epic fail that was its launch was kind of off-putting, but damn, Hello Games deserves mega props for sticking with it, eventually delivering what they originally promised, and as of this review, much more.  The scale of this game still astonishes me even after 60 hours. There's so many solar systems to visit, so many planets to explore and even if before the Origins update they all shared some assets it was still exciting to find that paradise planet that would be perfect to base on (Only to be let down because it has high sentinel activity :c ).  The gameplay is good. Nothing exceptional but it does the job and makes sure to make a point of travelling a lot.  The graphics in this game are great, the detail of the planets even better, but best of all is the atmosphere. Standing on a cliff looking off into the ocean, knowing that it's almost guaranteed you will be the only person to ever see this particular view even if there are many like it.  It extends far beyond this though, because if you ever get the chance to play the game in VR it becomes one of the best VR experiences I've had. Actually *playing* the game becomes more exhausting while you're in VR but every once in a while I'll load up my main save and just go sightseeing or flying around in my ship. Suddenly you realise the size and depth of things you didn't before on a monitor and it all becomes so much more immersive. You see the planets in the same way you would were you actually there.  Overall, I can highly recommend this game. It is a stunning example of what games are capable of these days and I thank Hello Games once again for not giving up.
